passages.source_text: ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἀκούων ταῦτα ὑπὸ συμπαθείας ἐδάκρυσεν, καὶ εὐθέως τοῖς συνοῦσιν γνησίοις ἔφη Ταῦτα εἴ τις πεπόνθει ἐν θεοσεβείᾳ, οἷα ὁ τούτου πέπονθεν πατήρ: εὐθέως τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ τὴν αἰτίαν προσῆπτεν ἐπιγράφων τὸν πονηρόν· οὕτω καὶ τοῖς ταλαιπώροις ἔθνεσιν συμβαίνει πάσχειν, καὶ ἀγνοοῦμεν οἱ θεοσεβεῖς. ταλαιπώρους δὲ αὐτοὺς εὐλόγως εἴρηκα, ὅτι ἐνταῦθα ἁλῶνται καὶ τῆς ἐκεῖ ἐλπίδος οὐ τυγχάνουσιν. οἱ γὰρ ἐν. θεοσεβείᾳ πάσχοντες τὰ θλιβερὰ εἰς ἔκπραξιν παραπτωμάτων πάσχουσιν.

ταῦτα τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος εἷς τις τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν τολμήσας ἀντὶ πάντων παρεκάλεσεν αὐτὸν αὔριον ὀρθριαίτερον εἰς Ἄραδον τὴν κατέναντι νῆσον εἰσπλεῦσαι, τριάκοντα οἶμαι οὐδ’ ὅλους ἀπέχουσαν σταδίους, ὡς ἐπὶ ἱστορίᾳ τῶν ἐκεῖ ἀμπελίων δύο στύλων μέγιστα ἐχόντων πάχη. ὁ οὖν πειθήνιος Πέτρος συνεχώρησεν εἰπὼν Ἐπὰν τοῦ πλοίου ἐκβῆτε, μὴ ἅμα πολλοὶ εἰσέρχεσθε εἰς τὴν θεωρίαν ὧν ἐπιθυμεῖτε· οὐ γὰρ βούλομαι στρέμματα γίνεσθαι εἰς ἡμᾶς τῶν πολιτῶν. καὶ οὕτως πλεύσαντες ῥοπῇ ὥρας κατήχθημεν εἰς τὴν νῆσον. ἐκβάντες δὲ τοῦ σκάφους εἰσήειμεν ἔνθα οἱ ἀμπέλινοι στύλοι ἦσαν, ὁμῶς ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἄλλος ἄλλο τι τῶν Φειδίου ἔργων ἐθεώρει.

Πέτρος δὲ μόνος οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἡγήσατο ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκεῖ ἱστορίαν γενέσθαι, γυναικὶ δέ τινι ἔξω πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν καθεζομένῃ καὶ τροφῆς χάριν μεταιτούσῃ πυκνὰ κατανοήσας ἔφη Γύναι, τί σοι τῶν μελῶν λείπει, ὅτι τοσαύτην ὕβριν ἀνεδέξω (λέγω δὴ τὸ προσαιτεῖν) καὶ μὴ μᾶλλον ταῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ σοι δεδωρημέναις χερσὶν ἐργαζομένη τὰς ἐφημέρους πορίζεις τροφάς; ἡ δὲ στενάξασα ἀπεκρίνατο Εἴθε γὰρ ἦσάν μοι χεῖρες ὑπουργεῖν δυνάμεναι· νῦν δέ μοι σχῆμα μόνον χειρῶν φυλάσσουσιν, νεκραὶ τυγχάνουσαι, ὑπὸ δηγμάτων ἐμῶν βεβασανισμέναι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἐπύθετο Τίς δὲ ἡ αἰτία τοῦ σὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν τοῦτο πεπονθέναι; ἡ δὲ ἀπεκρίνατο Ψυχῆς ἀσθένεια καὶ πλέον οὐθέν· εἰ γὰρ ἀνδρεῖον εἶχον φρόνημα, ἦν κρημνός, ἦν βυθός, ὅθεν ἐμαυτὴν ῥίψασα τῶν ὀδυνώντων με παύσασθαι ἠδυνάμην κακῶν.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί οὖν οἴει, γύναι; ὅτι πάντως οἱ ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς κολάσεως ἀπαλλάσσονται ἢ μὴ τῇ χείρονι κολάσει ἐν ᾅδῃ αἱ τῶν οὕτως θνησκόντων ψυχαὶ περὶ τῆς αὐτοκτονίας κολάζονται; ἡ δὲ ἔφη Εἴθε ἐπεπείσμην ὅτι ὄντως ἐν ᾅδῃ ψυχαὶ εὑρίσκονται ζῶσαι, καὶ ἠγάπων τῆς κολάσεως καταφρονήσασα θανεῖν, ὅπως τοὺς ἐμοὺς περιποθήτους ἴδω κἂν μίαν ὥραν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί ἄρα ἐστὶν τὸ λυποῦν σε, μαθεῖν ἤθελον, γύναι. ἐὰν γάρ με διδάξῃς, ἀντὶ ταύτης τῆς χάριτος πληροφορήσω σε ὅτι ἐν ᾅδῃ ζῶσιν αἱ ψυχαί, καὶ ἀντὶ κρημνοῦ ἢ βυθοῦ φάρμακον δώσω, ὅπως ἀβασανίστως τοῦ ζῆν τὸν βίον μεταλλάξαι δυνηθῇς.

καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τὸ ἀμφιβόλως ῥηθὲν μὴ · συνεῖσα, ἐπὶ τῇ ὑποσχέσει ἡσθεῖσα τοῦ λέγειν ἤρξατο οὕτως Γένος μὲν καὶ πατρίδα εἰπεῖν οὐκ οἶμαι πεῖσαί ποτε δυνηθῆναί τινα. πλὴν καὶ σοὶ τί διαφέρει τοῦτο μαθεῖν ἢ μόνην τὴν αἰτίαν, ἧς ἕνεκεν ὀδυνωμένη δήγμασιν τὰς ἐμὰς ἐνέκρωσα χεῖρας; πλὴν τὰ κατ’ ἐμαυτὴν ὡς δυνατὸν ἀκοῦσαί σε, διηγήσομαι. ἐγὼ πάνυ εὐγενὴς ὑπάρχουσα δυνάστου τινὸς προσταγῇ ἀνδρὶ πρὸς γένους αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντι ἐγενόμην γυνή. καὶ μετὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἔσχον ἕτερον υἱόν. ὁ δὲ τοῦ ἐμοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἀδελφὸς μανεὶς οὐχ ἔλαττον ἠράσθη μου τῆς ταλαιπώρου, σφόδρα σωφρονεῖν ἀγαπώσης. καὶ βουλομένη μήτε τῷ ἐραστῇ συνθέσθαι μήτε τῷ ἐμῷ ἀνδρὶ ἀναθέσθαι τὸν τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς ἐμὲ ἔρωτα, ἐλογισάμην, ἵνα μήτε μοιχησαμένη ἐμαυτὴν μιάνω μήτε τοῦ ἐμοῦ ἀνδρὸς τὴν κοίτην ὑβρίσω μήτε τῷ ἀδελφῷ τὸν ἀδελφὸν πολέμιον καταστήσω μήτε ὅλον γένος μέγα ὂν εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν πᾶσιν ὑποβάλω·— ὡς ἔφην, ἐλογισάμην τὴν πόλιν μετὰ τῶν ἐμῶν διδύμων παίδων ἐκβῆναι ἐπὶ χρόνον τινά, ἕως ἂν καὶ ὁ μιαρὸς ἔρως παύσηται τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμῇ ὕβρει κολακεύοντός με. τὸν μέντοι ἕτερον υἱὸν παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ μεῖναι εἰς παραμυθίαν κατέλιπον.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: But Peter, on hearing this, wept out of sympathy and immediately said to his genuine companions, “If anyone had suffered these things while living in reverence for God—the kinds of things this man’s father has suffered—he would immediately have attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God, naming the evil one as responsible. So too it happens that the wretched nations suffer, and we who revere God are unaware of it. I have rightly called them wretched, because they wander here and do not obtain the hope there. For those who suffer distressing things while living in reverence for God suffer them as payment exacted for transgressions.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: wept out of sympathy
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves συμπάθεια as compassionate fellow-feeling rather than merely sadness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his genuine companions
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνήσιοι characterizes those accompanying Peter as genuine or faithful; “genuine” retains the explicit adjective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ τὴν αἰτίαν προσῆπτεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος may mean teaching, account, or rationale; “teaching” fits the religious context, while the construction depicts attaching the cause to it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: naming the evil one as responsible
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιγράφω can mean inscribe, designate, or attribute; here it identifies the evil one as responsible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wretched nations
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔθνη may mean nations, peoples, or, in a religious contrast, Gentiles. “Nations” preserves the broader wording without excluding the contextual sense “Gentiles.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: they wander here
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁλῶνται is understood as the contracted present form of ἀλάομαι, “wander.” Contextually this may imply straying or wandering in error, but it does not denote being caught or convicted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as payment exacted for transgressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔκπραξις denotes exaction or collection of what is due, here presenting suffering as payment associated with transgressions.

source_issues.issue: The verified print places a full stop inside the prepositional phrase. The surviving words support reading ἐν with θεοσεβείᾳ continuously; treating the stop as intrusive editorial or printing punctuation is provisional but requires no missing text.

The verified printed form has rough breathing. It is interpreted as the contracted present of ἀλάομαι, “wander,” without altering the supplied spelling; the breathing is treated as a disclosed orthographic feature, not evidence for a capture-related verb.

passages.text: After Peter had said this, one of our company dared to speak for everyone and urged him to sail earlier the next morning to Aradus, the island opposite, which I think was not even a full thirty stadia away, to view the two vinewood columns there, which were of enormous thickness. Peter, being accommodating, agreed and said, “When you disembark from the ship, do not go in all at once as a large group to see the things you desire. I do not want the citizens turning toward us.” So we sailed and, in a fraction of an hour, put in at the island. After getting out of the boat, we went in to where the vinewood columns stood; and at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἷς τις τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν τολμήσας ἀντὶ πάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: one of our company dared to speak for everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The act supplied by τολμήσας is implicit; speaking is supported by the following request, while ἀντὶ πάντων means on behalf of all.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to view
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορία here denotes inspection or sightseeing, not the writing of history.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the two vinewood columns there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμπέλινος describes something made from or associated with a vine; “vinewood” preserves the material image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ βούλομαι στρέμματα γίνεσθαι εἰς ἡμᾶς τῶν πολιτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not want the citizens turning toward us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source-transparent wording treats στρέμματα as turnings directed toward the visitors. In context this may mean attracting the citizens’ attention or causing them to turn and look; “the citizens turning against us,” implying hostility or disturbance, is also possible but is not required by the noun itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a fraction of an hour
lexical_decisions.rationale: ῥοπή can denote a brief turn or moment; the phrase indicates a short portion of an hour, with “in a moment” also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἄλλος ἄλλο τι τῶν Φειδίου ἔργων ἐθεώρει
lexical_decisions.chosen: at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The distributive ἄλλος ἄλλο τι is explicit. The referent of αὐτοῖς may be the columns or other members of the party, so the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

passages.text: Peter alone did not consider it necessary to go and view the sights there. But after watching closely for some time a woman who was sitting outside, in front of the doors, and begging for food, he said, “Woman, what limb are you missing, that you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity—I mean begging—instead of working with the hands God has given you to obtain your daily food?” She groaned and replied, “If only I had hands capable of working! But now they retain only the form of hands, since they are dead, tortured by my own bites.” Peter asked, “What is the cause of your having suffered this terrible thing?” She answered, “Weakness of soul, and nothing more. For if I had possessed a courageous resolve, a cliff was there, and so was the deep; from there I could have thrown myself and gained relief from the evils that cause me pain.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκεῖ ἱστορίαν γενέσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to go and view the sights there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορία again denotes personal observation or sightseeing, and γενέσθαι with ἐπί conveys going for that purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after watching closely for some time
lexical_decisions.rationale: πυκνά can indicate repeated or sustained attention, while κατανοέω denotes attentive observation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕβρις here denotes degrading treatment or humiliation rather than merely pride; ἀναδέχομαι presents her as taking it upon herself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hands capable of working
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπουργεῖν literally means to serve or render assistance; in context it means functioning for useful work.

lexical_decisions.chosen: tortured by my own bites
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive ἐμῶν identifies the bites as hers, preserving the image of self-inflicted biting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Weakness of soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: ψυχή may denote soul, life, or inner self; “soul” retains the author’s psychological and moral terminology.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a cliff was there, and so was the deep
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated imperfect ἦν presents the available means of death. A counterfactual English alternative would be “there would have been a cliff and the deep.”

passages.text: Peter said, “What then do you think, woman? That those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment? Or are the souls of those who die in this way not punished in Hades with a worse punishment for their suicide?” She said, “If only I were convinced that souls really are found alive in Hades! Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment, so that I might see my dearly missed ones, even for a single hour.” Peter said, “I wanted to learn what it is that grieves you, woman. For if you tell me, in return for this favor I will fully assure you that souls live in Hades, and instead of a cliff or the deep I will give you a drug, so that you may be able, without torment, to exchange the life you are living.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντως οἱ ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς κολάσεως ἀπαλλάσσονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως supplies the categorical force, while ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτούς explicitly refers to taking one’s own life.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Or are ... not punished ... with a worse punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative μή is retained in the rhetorical alternative rather than being smoothed away, although the resulting English question is marked.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἠγάπων τῆς κολάσεως καταφρονήσασα θανεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγαπάω with an infinitive can express being pleased or willing to do something; “gladly” conveys that idiomatic force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my dearly missed ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπόθητος describes people intensely longed for; “dearly missed” leaves their precise relationship unstated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will fully assure you
lexical_decisions.rationale: πληροφορέω here means to bring someone to full assurance or conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a drug
lexical_decisions.rationale: φάρμακον can mean a medicine, remedy, or poison. “Drug” preserves the ambiguity essential to the woman’s subsequent misunderstanding.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀβασανίστως τοῦ ζῆν τὸν βίον μεταλλάξαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: without torment, to exchange the life you are living
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεταλλάσσω τὸν βίον can suggest either changing one’s manner of life or departing from life. The deliberately unusual English preserves the double sense rather than deciding between cure and death.

passages.text: The woman, not understanding what had been said ambiguously, was delighted by the promise and began to speak as follows: “As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them. But what difference does it make to you whether you learn that or only the reason why, in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them? Nevertheless, I will relate my own affairs as far as it is possible for you to hear them. I was of very noble birth, and at the command of a certain ruler I became the wife of a man related to him by blood. After having twin children, I had another son. But my husband’s brother went mad and fell no less deeply in love with me, unfortunate as I was and deeply devoted to chastity. Since I wanted neither to consent to my would-be lover nor to disclose to my husband his brother’s desire for me, I formed a plan so that I would neither defile myself by committing adultery, nor violate my husband’s bed, nor make brother an enemy to brother, nor subject the entire family, a prominent one, to everyone’s reproach. As I said, I resolved to leave the city with my twin children for a time, until the vile passion of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me should also cease. I did, however, leave my other son with his father as a consolation.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what had been said ambiguously
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμφιβόλως explicitly identifies Peter’s preceding statement as having a double or uncertain sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γένος μὲν καὶ πατρίδα εἰπεῖν οὐκ οἶμαι πεῖσαί ποτε δυνηθῆναί τινα
lexical_decisions.chosen: As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τινα as the subject of δυνηθῆναι and supplies the woman as the understood object of πεῖσαι, favoring reluctance to disclose in light of her following question. Alternatively, τινα may be the object of πεῖσαι and the woman the understood subject of δυνηθῆναι: “As for stating my lineage and homeland, I do not think I could ever convince anyone.” That reading emphasizes anticipated disbelief, possibly because her present condition contrasts with her claimed noble birth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀδυνωμένη δήγμασιν τὰς ἐμὰς ἐνέκρωσα χεῖρας
lexical_decisions.chosen: in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them
lexical_decisions.rationale: δήγμασιν is taken instrumentally with ἐνέκρωσα, while ὀδυνωμένη describes her anguished condition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as far as it is possible for you to hear them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording limits how much of her circumstances she will disclose; “as much as you are able to hear” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a man related to him by blood
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς γένους indicates kinship, and αὐτῷ most naturally refers to the ruler.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fell no less deeply in love with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek retains a negative comparison without stating its standard. The English preserves “no less” rather than replacing the litotes entirely with a positive intensifier.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deeply devoted to chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονεῖν here concerns sexual restraint and honorable conduct, while ἀγαπάω expresses her strong commitment to it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: neither to consent to my would-be lover
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι means agree or consent; “would-be lover” makes clear that his desire had not been accepted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor to disclose to my husband
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνατίθημι can mean refer, report, or entrust a matter to someone; “disclose” fits the concealed proposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμῇ ὕβρει κολακεύοντός με
lexical_decisions.chosen: of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕβρις may imply dishonor, outrage, or sexual violation. “Dishonor” is contextually defensible while leaving the more forceful alternatives disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a consolation
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραμυθία denotes comfort or consolation, explaining why one son remained with his father.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
